title: Value Projection — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Value Vector Generation and Information Transfer in Attention · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Beginner-to-advanced visual learning.
hero:
VALUE PROJECTION · VISUAL OVERVIEW

Attention finds information. Values carry what gets passed along.

Hidden token features are converted into Value vectors by a learned matrix, then blended according to attention weights.

questions.stem: What is Value Projection in a Transformer, and how does it convert each token's hidden representation into a Value vector containing information that can be passed to other tokens through the Attention Mechanism?
questions.figure:
VISUAL EXPLANATION

A learned matrix turns a hidden state into a Value vector

The projection learns which features of each token can be shared through attention.
options: Value projection sends original words directly between token positions without numerical transformations, so attention does not learn which features should be passed onward.

Value projection turns each token's hidden state into learned content features. After attention uses Queries and Keys to calculate weights, it combines the corresponding Values into contextual outputs.
Value projection measures how far apart token positions are and decides which future words must be hidden, rather than carrying information for output.
Value projection assigns positions to Query and Key vectors while leaving token content unchanged, confusing positional encoding with the content-carrying Value transformation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Value projection turns each token's hidden state into learned content features. After attention uses Queries and Keys to calculate weights, it combines the corresponding Values into contextual outputs. Imagine a film director choosing footage for a documentary. The director decides which scenes matter, but the actual content comes from the recorded clips. In attention, Values are similar to the information to be collected. A learned matrix turns each token's current representation into a Value vector. Query-Key comparisons decide the weights, then attention combines those Value vectors.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: The token's hidden representation X is mapped through learnable parameters W_V to a Value vector V=XW_V, optionally adding bias. Value features represent information that attention can send to other tokens. Queries and Keys determine the attention scores, while Values supply what is aggregated. These vectors are learned features, not literal word strings.

questions.stem: If Query vectors determine what information a token is looking for and Key vectors help identify relevant tokens, what exactly do Value vectors contribute, and why are they necessary for producing meaningful Attention outputs?
questions.figure:
VISUAL EXPLANATION

Queries and Keys find information; Values deliver it

Q and K determine which sources matter. V supplies the information to combine.
options: Queries provide the final answer content while Values only decide which source token receives attention, reversing the roles of matching and information transfer.
Values calculate similarities between tokens, while Keys store the completed context vector after attention has finished, so the two responsibilities are reversed.
Keys supply the output content and Values decide which words are allowed by the mask, even though matching and information transfer are separate processes.
Queries and Keys determine how relevant candidate positions are; Values contain the features to pass forward. Attention does not return the raw Key scores as its final contextual content.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Queries and Keys determine how relevant candidate positions are; Values contain the features to pass forward. Attention does not return the raw Key scores as its final contextual content. Picture a librarian helping someone research volcanoes. The visitor's request resembles a Query, catalog tags resemble Keys, and the book passages resemble Values. Queries and Keys help identify relevant sources, but their scores are not the information being returned. Values provide that information. A Transformer learns separate projections for all three roles.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Queries ask what the current token should attend to, and Keys determine which source tokens are relevant. Their dot products form attention scores, normalized by Softmax after masking where needed. Values carry the information being aggregated according to those weights. With fixed Q and K, changing V changes the output without changing the attention weights.

questions.stem: Consider the sentence "The chef prepared a delicious meal." How does a Transformer use Attention weights to collect information from Value vectors, and what happens when a token assigns different levels of importance to "chef," "prepared," and "meal"?
questions.figure:
VISUAL EXPLANATION

Chef, prepared, and meal contribute different amounts

A larger attention weight lets that source's Value contribute more to the result.
options: Attention scores only rearrange the original words into a new order, and the Value vectors are ignored before the model makes its final output.
Every token contributes exactly the same amount of Value information, even when the learned attention weights assign very different importance to their positions.
For each Query, multiply every allowed Value vector by its attention weight and add the results. Large weights contribute more information, though smaller weights can still affect the output.
The highest attention score always discards all other Value vectors completely, even though Softmax normally mixes several weighted sources into each output.
questions.explanation: Explanation: For each Query, multiply every allowed Value vector by its attention weight and add the results. Large weights contribute more information, though smaller weights can still affect the output. Read “The chef prepared a delicious meal.” When representing “prepared,” the network may assign different weights to “chef” and “meal.” Each source token has a Value vector containing learned features. Attention multiplies each Value by its corresponding weight and sums the results. A large weight gives a source more influence, but smaller weights need not become zero.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: For 'The chef prepared a delicious meal.', imagine weights for chef 0.20, prepared 0.30 and meal 0.50 and illustrative Values [1,0], [0,2], [2,1]. The weighted context becomes 0.2[1,0]+0.3[0,2]+0.5[2,1]=[1.2,1.1]. Actual learned model weights differ by target token, mask, layer and attention head; these are invented numbers to illustrate weighted aggregation.

questions.stem: How does the equation \(V = XW_V\) generate Value vectors from input hidden states, and how are these vectors combined with Softmax Attention weights through the operation \(\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})V\) to produce context-aware representations?
questions.figure:
VISUAL EXPLANATION

From XWᵥ and Softmax to the weighted context vector

A learned matrix produces Values. Softmax supplies weights, and weighted mixing builds context.
options: Compute V = XWV from hidden states, then A = softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ + mask) and output = AV. V determines content, while Q and K determine the mixing weights.
Values come from simply normalizing hidden states without learned weights, while the attention output uses Queries directly and never combines Value content.
Value vectors are calculated by adding Queries and Keys before the output projection assigns positions, reversing how learned Q, K, and V are produced.
Attention uses raw unnormalized Query-Key scores to combine Values directly, without Softmax or scaling, so its weights never form a probability distribution.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Compute V = XWV from hidden states, then A = softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ + mask) and output = AV. V determines content, while Q and K determine the mixing weights. Suppose a Transformer processes an announcement with T words, each represented by eight features. A learned matrix transforms X[T,8] into V[T,4]. Queries and Keys create matching scores, which are divided by a scale and passed through Softmax. The resulting weights multiply the Value matrix, producing contextual features for each Query position. This is the idea behind Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: With row-vector notation, learnable W_V maps input hidden states X to Values V=XW_V. Scaled dot-product attention calculates A=softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k), including appropriate masking, then A V. For X=[[1,2],[0,1]] and W_V=[[2,0],[1,1]], V=[[4,2],[1,1]]. One target with attention weights [0.25,0.75] receives [1.75,1.25]. The Values are feature coordinates, not probabilities.

questions.stem: How can Value Projection be implemented using Python and PyTorch, including creating a learnable Value projection layer, reshaping Value tensors across multiple Attention Heads, applying Attention weights, and examining how changing Value vectors affects the final Attention output?
questions.figure:
VISUAL EXPLANATION

Implement Value Projection and head reshaping in PyTorch

PyTorch learns the Value projection. Each head can mix separate Value features.
options: Value vectors are fixed random constants that never change through learning, so changing them cannot affect the output of a trained attention head.
Project hidden states with nn.Linear into Value features, reshape per head and use batched matrix multiplication A @ V. Inspect how changing a Value affects contextual output.
PyTorch creates only one Value vector for an entire sequence, no matter how many tokens exist, preventing position-specific attention content from being represented.
Attention weights are stored as fixed model parameters rather than calculated from Queries and Keys, so Values cannot be weighted differently for different inputs.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Project hidden states with nn.Linear into Value features, reshape per head and use batched matrix multiplication A @ V. Inspect how changing a Value affects contextual output. Imagine experimenting with a small PyTorch model that reads short weather alerts. Define nn.Linear to create Value vectors from token features. Organize the resulting tensor into attention heads and multiply each head's Values by its attention-weight matrix. Print the shapes and change one Value vector to see how the output changes. Values affect the content of the result, while Query-Key matching determines how strongly each source contributes.
questions.technicalExplanation:
Detailed explanation: A trainable nn.Linear generates the Value features. Splitting its output produces shape (batch=1,heads=2,tokens=3,features=2); attention weights have shape (1,2,3,3), giving a weighted result shaped (1,2,3,2). Since each normalized attention row sums to one, increasing every Value component by 0.5 increases every output component by 0.5 with the same Queries and Keys. These tensor shapes and this effect were checked locally in PyTorch. The example is unmasked and meant for demonstration, not autoregressive inference.
import math
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(7)
B, T, D, H = 1, 3, 4, 2
x = torch.randn(B, T, D)
q_layer = nn.Linear(D, D, bias=False)
k_layer = nn.Linear(D, D, bias=False)
v_layer = nn.Linear(D, D, bias=False)

def split(z):
    return z.reshape(B, T, H, D // H).transpose(1, 2)

q, k, v = split(q_layer(x)), split(k_layer(x)), split(v_layer(x))
scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(D // H)
weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
output = weights @ v
changed = weights @ (v + 0.5)
print(v.shape, weights.shape, output.shape)
print((changed - output).mean().item())  # 0.5
# Use a causal mask for decoder-only inference.

questions.stem: Why are Value vectors typically not rotated by Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), unlike Query and Key vectors, and how does Multi-Head Attention allow different Value projections to capture complementary information before their outputs are concatenated and transformed by the output projection?
questions.figure:
VISUAL EXPLANATION

RoPE rotates Q/K while different Value heads carry content

RoPE usually rotates Query and Key features; Values carry content from different heads.
options: Standard RoPE rotates Q and K, not V, because it changes positional matching. Different heads learn different Value features, which are concatenated and mixed by an output projection WO.
RoPE normally rotates all Value vectors while leaving Queries and Keys independent of position, so the attention scores cannot reflect relative distance.
Every attention head uses one identical Value vector, making concatenated head outputs necessarily equal and preventing different features from being transferred.
The output projection only inserts positions and cannot mix head features, so different Value projections would make no difference to attention.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Standard RoPE rotates Q and K, not V, because it changes positional matching. Different heads learn different Value features, which are concatenated and mixed by an output projection WO. Suppose a model reads an instruction about repairing a bicycle. One attention head may carry information about the damaged part, while another helps represent the required action. In standard RoPE, Queries and Keys receive rotations to represent relative position; Values normally do not. Multiple heads can use different learned Value projections to transfer complementary information.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: RoPE usually rotates Query and Key feature pairs by position-dependent angles. This changes how positional differences influence Query-Key matching. Values generally remain unrotated because their primary role is to pass content after those weights have been calculated. Multiple heads each learn separate projections, so their weighted Value outputs may capture complementary information. Outputs from all heads are concatenated and mixed by W_O. This is a common design choice, not a universal prohibition on Value transformations.

questions.stem: How do Value Projection and Value caching influence the memory requirements and inference performance of autoregressive Large Language Models, and how do architectures such as Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) manage the trade-offs between Value representation capacity, KV-cache size, memory bandwidth, and output quality?
questions.figure:
VISUAL EXPLANATION

KV-cache size varies across MHA, GQA, MQA, and MLA

Sharing or compressing Keys and Values reduces cache memory use, with possible trade-offs.
options: MQA duplicates its Value cache separately for every Query head, making its cache larger than standard MHA even when it shares a single Value head.
All attention architectures store independent full Keys and Values for every Query head during decoding, regardless of cache compression or head sharing.
MLA always creates a smaller cache than MQA under all settings, even though latent dimensions and implementation can change actual memory requirements.
MHA keeps separate Key/Value heads; GQA and MQA share KV across Queries, and MLA compresses cached representations. Compare memory, bandwidth, latency and quality on the target model.
questions.explanation: Explanation: MHA keeps separate Key/Value heads; GQA and MQA share KV across Queries, and MLA compresses cached representations. Compare memory, bandwidth, latency and quality on the target model. Picture an assistant generating a long equipment-maintenance report. During decoding, storing old Keys and Values helps it avoid recomputing earlier projections. In MHA, each attention head generally has separate KV representations. GQA shares them among groups of Query heads, while MQA shares one. MLA may cache compressed representations instead. The benefit is lower memory or bandwidth use, but representation capacity and output quality must still be tested.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Autoregressive inference caches earlier K/V data, so generating each new token can reuse history. With Hkv KV heads and equal Key and Value head dimension d, standard KV cache elements per token per layer are 2Hkv d. With 8 Query heads, d=64: MHA uses 1024, GQA with two KV heads uses 256, and MQA with one uses 128. An illustrative MLA design storing compressed latent width 128 and separate RoPE key width 32 stores 160. Actual MLA widths vary; it is not always smaller than MQA. These designs trade memory, bandwidth, compute and quality.
